messages.subject: Using A matrix with automatic intercept / intercepts and factor variables
parts:
Hi,

I have a question regarding the handling of intercepts, A-matrices, and factor variables in inla.

If you try to fit a model with an A matrix in control.predictor without removing the automatic intercept from the formula, you get a warning message like:
##... : The A-matrix in the predictor (see ?control.predictor)
is specified
## but an intercept is in the formula. This will likely result
## in the intercept being applied multiple times in the model, and is likely
## not what you want. See ?inla.stack for more information.
## You can remove the intercept adding “-1” to the formula.
I am a bit confused by this error message -- it says that it is *likely* that the intercept is applied multiple times but does not say whether it actually is. Is there any way to check if it actually is applied more than once? And if it is, is there any way to prevent it? I do not have any manual intercept in the model, so there should be no issue coming from that.

The above is my main question, but for some context:
The examples I have seen solve this warning by removing the automatic intercept with "-1" and then manually creating an intercept covariate. However, this does not seem to work in my case. I'll explain what I am trying to do in case my whole approach is wrong somehow.
I am trying to fit a model along the lines of
y ~ 1 + a + b + f(...) + f(...)
where a,b are categorical variables, and the f:s are rw2 and spde models with some replicates that I control with the A-matrix. Since a,b are factors I expect one level from each to be dropped to prevent identification/colinearity problems. This works just fine when the automatic intercept is included in the formula, but when I instead create a manual intercept and drop the automatic one it doesn't: all levels of a are kept. This seems to give problems with very large uncertainties in the estimates. Because of this it seems natural to me to use the automatic intercept, but this of course gives the warning above.

Here are some excerpts from the fixed effects estimates, where we see this phenomenon, note the very large sds for a with the manual intercept, and that level a1 is included.

messages.author: 9940b4fcc153c7d7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Using A matrix with automatic intercept / intercepts and factor variables
parts:
Hi,

I suggest just using a manual intercept, then you know what is going on. There are ways to check what you are doing when you make automatic choices, but it is unneccesarily intricate compared to just defining your choices manually.

With factors, what I prefer to do is
1. for small factors, define the 0-1 equivalents manually myself
2. for larger factors (4+ levels) define an iid effect over the factor levels

For your problme, think about the manual intercept as the "baseline" for the factor. Then all the factor levels describe a change from this baseline. If you do not specify a random effect shrinkage (iid effect), or remove one factor level, your model does not make any sense.

How the defaults for factors and intercept combinations interact with stack is unknown to me, so I suggest setting it up manually and not relying on automatic expansions when using stack.

Best,
Haakon

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Using A matrix with automatic intercept / intercepts and factor variables
parts: I've to add to Haakon's excellent advice and warn that the intercept is the bias of the random error and acts as the first moment of the model and thus removing it needs mathematical support. Removing it creates biased errors (even without space-time or other row based bias). I believe completeness, sufficiency, efficiency etc gets affected too ... Rudy

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Using A matrix with automatic intercept / intercepts and factor variables
parts:
Thanks for your email and comment.

In my view, it is more that in the simple model

y ~ 1 + x

then the intercept do what its supposed to do.

with the 'A' matrix, there the data depends on the linear predictor
eta*, where

eta* = A %*% eta

and eta is defined through the formula

y ~ 1 + x

then the intercept appears as an intercept in 'eta' and not as an
intercept in the 'eta*'. In most cases, this is not what the user want,
so this is why it is recommended not to use the '1' in the formula (ie
use '-1' instead), but define explicitely what you want.

H

On Fri, 2019-05-03 at 10:11 -0400, Aniruddha Banerjee wrote:
> I've to add to Haakon's excellent advice and warn that the intercept
> is the bias of the random error and acts as the first moment of the
> model and thus removing it needs mathematical support. Removing it
> creates biased errors (even without space-time or other row based
> bias). I believe completeness, sufficiency, efficiency etc gets
> affected too ... Rudy
>
> On Tue, Apr 30, 2019 at 7:41 AM Haakon Bakka <ba...@r-inla.org>
> wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > I suggest just using a manual intercept, then you know what is
> > going on. There are ways to check what you are doing when you make
> > automatic choices, but it is unneccesarily intricate compared to
> > just defining your choices manually.
> >
> > With factors, what I prefer to do is
> > 1. for small factors, define the 0-1 equivalents manually myself
> > 2. for larger factors (4+ levels) define an iid effect over the
> > factor levels
> >
> > For your problme, think about the manual intercept as the
> > "baseline" for the factor. Then all the factor levels describe a
> > change from this baseline. If you do not specify a random effect
> > shrinkage (iid effect), or remove one factor level, your model does
> > not make any sense.
> >
> > How the defaults for factors and intercept combinations interact
> > with stack is unknown to me, so I suggest setting it up manually
> > and not relying on automatic expansions when using stack.
> >
> > Best,
> > Haakon
